Grade 3 · Unit 3.2

Weather, Climate, and Hazards

What weather can we expect in different places and seasons, and how can we reduce harm from weather hazards?

Weather is what happens today, and climate is the pattern over many years. This unit shows how weather is measured, how graphs reveal seasonal patterns, why different places have different climates, and how designs can reduce the damage from storms and floods but never remove every risk.

In this lesson

  1. Weather is short-term; climate is long-term
  2. We measure weather
  3. Graphs show seasonal weather patterns
  4. Different regions have different climates
  5. Designs can reduce weather-hazard harm
  6. Try it at home or in class
  7. Check yourself
  8. Play: Weather, Climate, and Hazards Sort

Concept 1

Weather is short-term; climate is long-term

Weather is what happens today; climate is the pattern over many years.

Analogy

Your closet

Your clothes show the difference between today and “usually.”

“Weather is what you wear today. Climate is what your closet is ready for all year.”

In Michigan, the closet has a puffy winter coat, mittens, and rain boots for January, and shorts, a sun hat, and sandals for July. You do not wear all of them on one day. The closet shows what usually fits here.

Data

Daily vs monthly

One day’s high temperature compared with the average over many years.

“One day can be weird. Many years show climate.”

  • Seven made-up daily July highs: 78°F (26°C), 86°F (30°C), 81°F (27°C), 90°F (32°C), 75°F (24°C), 84°F (29°C), 83°F (28°C).
  • Dashed line: the typical Detroit July high, 83°F (28°C).

Concept 2

We measure weather

Scientists measure temperature, precipitation (rain, snow, sleet, or hail), wind, and clouds.

Try it

Rain gauge

A cup with a ruler measures how much rain falls.

“After rain, measure how deep the water is.”

You did this before / what is new: You noticed weather in K-B; now you measure it and record data.

Predict first: How deep will the water be after a rain? A little, or a lot?

You need:

  • A clear cup or jar with straight sides
  • A ruler
  • Tape
  • A pencil
  • Paper

What you do:

  • Tape the ruler on the cup with the 0 at the bottom.
  • Put it outside in an open spot, away from roofs and trees.
  • After it rains, read the line where the water stops, in centimeters (cm). 1 cm is a little less than half an inch.
  • Write the date and the number. Pour out the water.
  • Do it for at least five rainy days.

What you should see: You will get small numbers, such as 0.5 cm (about ¼ inch) one day and 1 cm (about ½ inch) another. Rain amounts change from day to day.

Why it matters: Weather people measure rain the same way so they can compare days and months. People in Michigan can use rain records like this to see how wet a spring or summer was.

Try it

Wind vane

A paper arrow on a pencil shows which way the wind blows.

“A wind vane points into the wind. The wind comes FROM that way. Put the tail on the other end.”

Predict first: Which way will the arrow point when the wind blows from the west?

You need:

  • A pencil with an eraser
  • A pin or thumbtack
  • A straw
  • Paper
  • Tape
  • A card with N, E, S, W

What you do:

  • Cut a paper arrowhead and a bigger tail. Tape them to the ends of a straw.
  • Push the pin through the middle of the straw into the pencil eraser.
  • Take it outside and hold it up. Use the card to find north.
  • Wait until it stops moving. The arrowhead points to where the wind comes FROM.

Notice: The big tail catches the wind and swings away, so the head points into the wind.

Why it matters: Knowing the wind direction helps us tell what weather may come next.

Real world

Weather report

Weather maps use small pictures.

“Symbols show rain, snow, sun, and wind.”

  • Sun: clear skies.
  • Rain: drops fall from clouds.
  • Snow: flakes fall when it is cold.
  • Wind: an arrow or flag shows which way the air is moving.

Look for these on the weather map the next time a TV weather person shows Michigan.

Concept 3

Graphs show seasonal weather patterns

Tables and graphs show typical weather by month or season.

Temperature and rain units: Freezing is 0°C, or 32°F. To guess °F from °C, double the °C and add 30 (a rough guess, close enough for weather). 1 inch is a little more than 2 cm (about 2½ cm).

Diagram

Monthly bar graph

Bars show the typical high for each month.

“July bars are tall. January bars are short.”

Find July (83°F, 28°C) and January (32°F, 0°C) on the bars.

Try it

Graph your class data

Students add their own temperatures or rain amounts to a graph.

“Make a bar for each month.”

You need:

  • A sheet of graph paper or a bar graph sheet with the months along the bottom
  • A pencil
  • A thermometer
  • A notebook

What you do:

  • Read the thermometer at the same time each school day for one or two weeks.
  • Write the temperature in °F and °C.
  • Draw one bar for each day or each month.
  • Find the warmest and coldest bars.

Concept 4

Different regions have different climates

Climate depends on location, including nearness to large lakes or oceans.

Diagram

Climate map

A simple picture of Earth with cold, mild, and hot regions.

“Near the equator is warmer. Near the poles is colder.”

Near the equator (the middle line around Earth), the Sun shines more directly, so it is warmer. Near the poles (the cold top and bottom ends of Earth), it is colder. Temperate means mild, not very hot or cold. Michigan is in the temperate band. Real climates also depend on oceans, mountains, and wind, so this is a simple picture.

Data

Region cards

Three cards describe a tropical place, a polar place, and a Michigan place.

“Combine the clues. What is usually true there?”

Three cards to read:

Tropical place (tropical means near the equator)

  • Hot all year.
  • Often rains a lot.
  • Plants grow all year.

Polar place

  • Cold all year.
  • Little snow or rain.
  • The ground is often frozen.

Michigan place

  • Hot summers, cold snowy winters.
  • Rain all year.

Try it: Cover the place names. Read only the clues and guess which place is which. Why did the clues work?

Real world

Michigan and the Great Lakes

Michigan touches four of the five Great Lakes: Superior, Michigan, Huron, and Erie.

“The Great Lakes make Michigan weather milder near shore and snowier in some places.”

Lake water warms and cools slowly, so shore towns are milder. Cold wind blowing across warmer lake water makes lake-effect snow, which is heavy snow that falls on land downwind of a lake.

Concept 5

Designs can reduce weather-hazard harm

A hazard is something that can cause harm, like a flood or a tornado. Solutions such as barriers, drains, and rules can reduce damage, but they cannot remove all risk.

Analogy

Helmet

A bicycle helmet is a design that reduces harm.

“A helmet does not stop falls. It reduces harm.”

What matches what: the helmet is the design (a barrier, a safe room, a strong roof). A fall is the hazard (a flood, a tornado, a storm). Neither stops the hazard from happening. Both make the harm smaller.

Try it

Barrier test

A flood barrier is a design that slows or blocks flood water. Pour water down a soil slope and test cardboard and foil barriers.

“Test barriers. Which one keeps soil in place?”

You did this before / what is new: You tested erosion guards in 2-C (erosion is water or wind carrying away soil); now the question is a design problem: which barrier reduces harm from a flood? The new measurement is spoonfuls of sediment moved (sediment is bits of soil and sand that water carries away), and you compare a no-barrier run with a cardboard fence and a grass model. One messy trial is not the finding: test each barrier several times the same way and compare before you claim.

Predict first: Which will keep more soil in place, a cardboard fence or a grass patch?

You need:

  • A tray with soil piled at one end
  • A cup
  • A spoon
  • Cardboard
  • Foil
  • A piece of sod or grass

What you do:

  • Tilt the tray a little. Pour one cup of water the same slow way each time.
  • Run one trial with no barrier. Count spoonfuls of soil (sediment) that washed to the low end.
  • Add one barrier and repeat. Keep the water and slope the same.
  • Run each barrier at least three times and take the middle number.

What you should see: With no barrier you might move about 8 spoonfuls, the same as the graph in the Hands-on section below. A barrier should move fewer. Your numbers will differ.

Why it matters: Engineers can test small models like this before they build something to protect a river bank or shoreline.

Data

Before/after erosion

The sediment moved with and without a barrier.

“Less sediment means the barrier helped.”

  • No barrier: 8 spoonfuls.
  • Cardboard fence: 5 spoonfuls.
  • Grass model: 2 spoonfuls.

Each number is from one run. The bar graph is in the Hands-on section below.

Which barrier moved the least soil?

Try it

Claim frame

Fill in a sentence frame on paper.

“I claim ___ reduces harm from ___ because our data show ___.”

Example: I claim the grass model reduces harm from flooding because our data show it moved 2 spoonfuls of soil, but no barrier moved 8.

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Test a flood-barrier design. Use the same amount of water each time. Compare how much soil moves. Then write: “I claim ___ reduces harm from flooding because our data show ___.”

Try it

What you need

  • Clear cup or jar with straight sides (not a paper cup)
  • Ruler, tape, pencil with an eraser, paper, straw
  • Pin or thumbtack, card with N, E, S, W
  • Shallow tray, soil or sand, a cup, a spoon, cardboard or foil, a piece of sod or grass

Safety: wash hands after soil or sand trays. Keep trays and water away from Chromebooks, wipe up spills, and let an adult control how much water is poured.

Try it

What you do

  • Make the rain gauge and wind vane and put them outside (15 minutes).
  • Record the weather for a week: sky, wind direction, rain in cm (or inches).
  • Make a bar graph from your numbers or the Michigan table (15 minutes).
  • Read the three climate cards. Match each to a place (10 minutes).
  • Test one barrier against no barrier with the same water each time (20 minutes).

Notice: One day does not show climate. Many days, over many years, do.

Why it matters: You use measurements to describe weather and to check whether a design reduces harm.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but collect your own when you can.

Barrier results (one run each):

  • No barrier: 8 spoonfuls.
  • Cardboard fence: 5 spoonfuls.
  • Grass model: 2 spoonfuls.

For temperature and precipitation, use the Detroit table in the Michigan weather table above.

These are one run each, so a different tray can give different counts. Repeat each barrier at least three times and take the middle number.

Near you: Watch the sky and the wind where you live. What is the weather today? What is this month usually like in Michigan?

Words to know

weather
short-term condition of the air.
climate
typical weather over a long time.
temperature
how hot or cold something is.
precipitation
rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
wind
moving air.
season
part of the year with typical weather patterns.
pattern
something that repeats.
data
information collected.
hazard
something that can cause harm.
flood barrier
a design that slows or blocks flood water.
erosion
water or wind carrying away soil.
sediment
bits of soil and sand that water carries away.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, limits, pacing

Pacing: five 30-minute sessions.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Weather and climate are the same.” Correct: weather is short-term; climate is long-term.
  • “One cold day means climate changed.” Correct: climate needs long-term patterns.
  • “Seasons happen because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer.” Correct: tilt causes seasons; detailed cause comes later.
  • “Clouds make cold.” Correct: clouds can block sunlight or trap heat.
  • “Hazards cannot be reduced.” Correct: designs can reduce harm, but they cannot eliminate all risk.

Limits and cautions:

  • This unit does not fully teach the water cycle; Unit 4 does that.
  • It does not teach climate change; later units handle human impact.
  • Cause of seasons is simplified here and handled more fully later.
  • Barrier tests are models; real flood control involves engineering, land use, and public policy.
  • Detroit values are typical normals. Check them against NOAA NCEI 1991-2020 climate normals before publishing (verify).
  • Other units (4.5, 5.4) use their own trays, so their numbers do not belong to this table.
  • What is new here: 2-C counted finger widths of sand; this slope test counts spoonfuls and asks which barrier cuts harm from a flood.
  • The rain gauge goal is at least five rainy days (Concept 2). The week of weather records in the Hands-on block is separate.

Connections: Builds on: K-B Sunlight, Weather, and Staying Safe; Unit 0: How Science Works. Builds toward: 5.4 Earth’s Spheres, Water, and Communities; Unit 4 Weather & the Water Cycle; Unit 6 Natural Hazards.
